arguments.content:
Here are some hobbies for birdwatchers looking to branch out and meet people outside the birding world, ordered from most to least expensive to get started.

Horseback riding is a fantastic outdoor hobby with a strong social culture. Barns are tight-knit communities, and group trail rides and lesson programs make it easy to bond with people over shared learning. Expect to spend around $1,500 to $4,000 to get started with lessons, basic gear, and riding boots.

Scuba diving opens up an entirely different outdoor world and has one of the most welcoming beginner communities out there. Dive shops run group certification courses, and dive clubs are social by nature since buddy diving is a must. Start-up costs run roughly $1,000 to $2,500 for certification and basic equipment.

Kayaking or canoeing gets you on the water and into paddling clubs, where social outings and weekend river trips are the norm. It's a great way to spend time outdoors with people whose main interest is paddling, not identifying warblers. Budget around $700 to $1,800 for a decent入门 kayak, paddle, and personal flotation device.

Outdoor photography has plenty of overlap with the observational skills birders already have, but landscape, street, and macro photography communities are entirely different crowds. Photo walks and meet-up groups are common in most cities. A solid entry-level mirrorless camera setup runs about $500 to $1,500.

Gardening and community garden plots put you outdoors and surrounded by people passionate about food, flowers, and soil. Community gardens especially are social hubs where neighbors become friends. Seed-starting costs and basic tools come to around $200 to $600.

Amateur astronomy draws night-owl crowds to star parties, dark-sky meetups, and observatory events — all outdoors, all very social, and the Venn diagram with birders is surprisingly small. A decent beginner telescope and accessories will set you back roughly $250 to $800.

Trail running has an incredibly approachable community. Local running groups organize weekly trail runs, and the post-run socializing is half the appeal. The outdoors aspect is obvious, and the only real investment is a pair of trail shoes, making start-up costs around $100 to $200.

Outdoor yoga and tai chi classes are held in parks and draw a broad, mixed crowd. They're low-pressure social environments where you can chat before and after class, and you'll meet plenty of people whose interests have nothing to do with birds. Mats and basic gear cost roughly $30 to $100.

Hiking meet-up groups through apps like Meetup or local outdoor clubs are one of the easiest ways to get outdoors and socialize with a wide range of people. Hiking requires very little gear beyond what most birders already own — sturdy shoes, a water bottle, and a daypack — so start-up costs are around $20 to $80 if you need to grab a pair of hiking shoes.
